verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, a maskil, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster; to be sung to the strings. A maskil, a song of insight, David's.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a stage direction. The psalm is handed to the master of song, who sets it to strings, so that a cry first made in hiding among the Ziphites is now sung aloud in the sanctuary. KJV 'chief Musician' hides how plain the root is: למנצח is from נצח 'to oversee', and the word names the one who directs the singing. 'Neginoth' (KJV) is not a place or a tune but the stringed instruments themselves, from the root for striking the strings. 'Maschil' (KJV) is simply transliterated because no one is sure of its meaning; it is best heard as a song that teaches. The 'of David' is a label of belonging, and the next verse gives the incident the psalm recalls. In the Hebrew numbering this heading is verse 1, which is why the KJV verse numbers run one or two behind from here.

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to have insight, to act wisely'. A heading used for several psalms; whether it names a genre, a teaching or a skilful song is not settled. The Targum renders it 'good insight' (שִׂכְלָא טָבָא).
A participle with the article, 'the one who oversees', here the leader of the music.

verses.translation_literal: In the coming of the Ziphites, and they said to Saul, "Is not David hiding himself with us?"
verses.translation_dramatic: The Ziphites came. They came to Saul, and they said: "Is David not hiding among us?"
verses.directors_commentary: The heading tells you the moment: David is a fugitive, the people of Ziph are men of the hill country of Judah, and they go to Saul with word of where he is. The Hebrew question הֲלֹא is a leading one, 'Isn't it so that...?', and it expects the answer yes. The text gives no motive for the informers; whether they thought they were doing the king a service or saw their own advantage is the actor's interpretation, not the Hebrew's. Meiri adds that David had been hiding among them and trusting them, which sharpens the betrayal. The KJV 'Ziphims' carries a Hebrew plural ending into English; 'Ziphites' is the people of the town. The verb מִסְתַּתֵּר is a reflexive participle, 'hiding himself', a man in continuous concealment, not a man who ran once. Radak and Metzudat Zion identify the Ziphites simply as the men of the place Ziph, on the border of Judah, so they are David's own tribe. The scene behind it is told in 1 Samuel 23:19 and 26:1.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael participle: 'hiding himself'. Metzudat David glosses it 'hiding with us', lodged among us.
The people of Ziph, a town in the hill country of Judah. Radak calls it a place on the border of Judah.

verses.translation_literal: God, by your name save me, and by your might judge me.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, by your name, save me. By your strength, set my cause right.
verses.directors_commentary: The cry begins with the one word that matters, 'God', placed first so that the prayer cannot be mistaken for a complaint. David is alone and outnumbered, with no army and no court to appeal to, so he appeals to the name, which in the ancient Near East means the whole standing and reputation of the one who bears it. To act 'by the name' is to act on the strength of who God has shown himself to be. The two halves match: 'save' (the root ישע, to bring out of a tight place) and 'judge' (דין). KJV 'judge me' sounds like a request to be put on trial, and an English reader may think David fears the verdict. In the Hebrew the sense is the opposite: Rashi explains it as 'take my vengeance', citing Deuteronomy 32:36, and Radak and Metzudat David say 'take my vengeance', that is, take up my case and decide it for me. So 'judge' here is to act as judge on David's side. The preposition בְּ can be 'by' or 'in'; the Hebrew uses the same בְּ in both lines, 'by your name... and by your might', and ASV's 'in thy might' is a possible choice of the second sense.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'you will judge me'. In the sense of taking up a person's case, as in Deuteronomy 32:36 ('the LORD will judge his people'); 'vindicate' conveys the sense. Rashi and Radak read it as obtaining redress.
'By your name': on the strength of the character and repute of God. Radak: 'by your name, which I have called upon'; Ibn Ezra: 'for the sake of your name'.

verses.translation_literal: God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, hear my prayer. Bend your ear to the words that leave my mouth.
verses.directors_commentary: The two lines say one thing twice, the Hebrew device of parallelism: 'hear' and 'give ear', 'prayer' and 'words of my mouth'. Do not play them as two different requests. Ibn Ezra and Radak notice a difference of register: 'my prayer' may be the inward prayer of the heart and 'the words of my mouth' the spoken speech, so David asks to be heard in both. 'Give ear' is a verb made from the noun 'ear', literally 'ear it'. The KJV 'give ear' keeps this, and BBE's 'let my prayer come before you' replaces the Hebrew's two imperatives with a softer wish. In the ancient world a petitioner who spoke aloud before a deity was making a legal appeal, so the stress on the mouth is deliberate: this is a spoken case.

philological_notes.note: A verb built on אֹזֶן 'ear': 'ear it!', 'turn your ear'. The ending -ah on the imperative adds urgency.
'Words of my mouth'. Ibn Ezra distinguishes the prayer of the heart from the speech of the tongue, and Radak allows that the two may be mere repetition.

verses.translation_literal: For strangers have risen up against me, and ruthless ones have sought my life; they have not set God before them. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: For strangers have risen against me, ruthless men who hunt my very life. They do not keep God before their eyes. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the reason for the prayer, introduced by 'for'. David names two kinds of enemy, 'strangers' and 'ruthless ones', and Ibn Ezra and Radak identify the second with the Ziphites. The point of 'strangers' is bitter: Metzudat David says the Ziphites are 'strangers' to Saul, not even his own family, and yet they rise up to hand David over to him. There is also an irony the KJV hides: 'strangers' (זָרִים) are by definition outsiders to the covenant, and these are the men of Judah, David's own tribe. KJV 'oppressors' is weaker than the Hebrew עָרִיצִים, which is a word for the terrifying, violent and tyrannical. And 'seek after my soul' misleads a modern reader: נֶפֶשׁ is the throat, the breath, the life, and to 'seek' it is to hunt a man to kill him. 'They have not set God before them' is the key charge, because the Hebrew שׂוּם לְנֶגֶד is to put in front of one's eyes as a guide; these men act as if no one is watching. Radak and Meiri read it as no fear of punishment. 'Selah' is a musical or liturgical marker whose meaning is lost; the singers may have paused or raised a loud instrumental note, and the KJV rightly leaves it untranslated.

philological_notes.note: 'Ruthless ones', terrifying and violent men; from the root 'to cause dread, to strike terror'. Radak treats 'strangers' and 'ruthless ones' as a doubling of the same idea in different words, while Ibn Ezra and Radak elsewhere identify the ruthless with the Ziphites.
'My life, my throat, my self'. Not an immortal 'soul' in the later sense; to seek it is to seek to kill.
A liturgical or musical marker of uncertain meaning. Malbim glosses it as 'the end of the matter'.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, God is a helper to me; the Lord is among those who sustain my life.
verses.translation_dramatic: But look: God is my helper. The Lord himself stands among those who hold up my life.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns on a single word, הִנֵּה, 'look!'. David has just described the circle closing on him, and now he points to a second presence in the room. Play it as a discovery said aloud, not as a doctrine. The second line is hard, and the commentators split. Ibn Ezra reports that Rabbi Moses (commonly identified as Moses ibn Chiquitilla) read it as 'the Lord alone is worth all the supporters', that is, equal to all of them together, not one among them. Radak and Meiri take 'those who sustain my life' as David's human allies, with the Lord helping them; Malbim says the Lord joins them to sustain David. I keep the grammar as the Hebrew has it, 'among'. KJV 'with them that uphold' is a fair rendering; ASV 'of them that uphold' is closer to the Hebrew preposition and more daring: the Lord is counted as one of David's supporters. Note that the two names change: the first line says אֱלֹהִים, the second אֲדֹנָי, 'my Lord', a title, not the name YHWH. The KJV prints 'the Lord' in lowercase here, while in verse 8 'LORD' in capitals translates YHWH, so the reader can tell the difference.

philological_notes.note: 'Among those who sustain / uphold'. The root סמך is to lean on, to prop, to support. The preposition בְּ is disputed: 'among' (the Lord is one of them), 'is the helper of' or 'with'. Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Malbim disagree on whether the supporters are human or divine.
'My Lord', the title. Radak: 'who is master over everything'.

verses.translation_literal: He will bring back the evil to my watchers; in your faithfulness, cut them off.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the evil they planned turn round and come home to those who watch me. In your faithfulness, silence them for good.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest line to say aloud, and the director should not soften it. David asks for a harsh reversal: the harm they devised will return on them, and then they will be cut off. A modern audience may flinch at a hero praying for destruction, but ancient justice works by return, 'the deed comes home', and the psalm grounds the request in God's 'faithfulness' (אֱמֶת), not in David's anger. Rashi says it plainly: because you are true, and you said you would punish slanderers and killers (Psalm 101:5), therefore cut them off. The KJV 'in thy truth' is right but a reader hears 'truth' as a fact; אֱמֶת is reliability, keeping one's word. The wordplay is in 'my watchers' (שׁוֹרְרַי): the root שׁוּר is 'to watch, to spy', and the KJV flattens it to 'enemies'. David has in mind the Ziphites who watch his hiding places and report them to Saul (Radak). The text also has a Ketiv and a Qere: the written form is 'it will return' and the reading is 'he will bring back'. Radak notes the sense is the same.

philological_notes.note: 'To my watchers', from the root 'to watch, observe, look closely'. Rashi links it to Numbers 24:17 ('I behold him, but not near'); Metzudat Zion says it has the sense of looking and seeing.
Qere: 'he will bring back' (hiphil, God as subject). Ketiv: 'it will return' (qal, the evil as subject). Radak says the sense is one.
'Cut them off, put an end to them'. Metzudat Zion compares Psalm 101:8.

verses.translation_literal: With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, YHWH, for it is good.
verses.translation_dramatic: With a willing heart I will bring my offering to you. I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, because it is good.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice lightens here. David moves from hiding to the altar, and the prayer ends in a vow of thanks. A נְדָבָה is a freewill offering, a gift that no law demanded, as opposed to the sacrifices that were required. Radak and Metzudat David read the word as the spirit in which it is given, 'with a generous and good spirit'; the ASV 'freewill-offering' and the KJV 'freely' each catch part of this. The verb אוֹדֶה is from a root that means both 'to thank' and 'to confess, to acknowledge publicly', so thanks in this world is spoken aloud before others. The divine name appears here for the first time in the psalm as YHWH, after 'God' and 'Lord' in the preceding verses; the KJV prints it 'LORD'. The closing 'for it is good' is ambiguous: is 'it' the name or the deliverance? Metzudat David says 'the name is good', and the Hebrew has no 'it', only the verb 'good'. A staging thought of my own: a freewill sacrifice is an animal given out of one's own flock or purse, and for a fugitive it is a real cost, so the vow is no small thing.

philological_notes.note: 'In willingness, voluntarily', a freewill offering, as opposed to an obligatory one. Radak and Metzudat David: 'with a generous spirit'.
'I will thank, I will acknowledge', a verb that both thanks and confesses. The object is 'your name'.

verses.translation_literal: For from every trouble he has delivered me, and on my enemies my eye has looked.
verses.translation_dramatic: For out of every trouble he has pulled me free, and my own eyes have looked upon my enemies.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends in the past tense, as though the rescue has already happened, a perfect verb used for something so certain that it is spoken as done. Metzudat David reads a double mercy: he saved me from every trouble they planned, and my eye also saw what it wished to see in them. That second line is bare in the Hebrew: 'my eye has looked on my enemies', with no object. KJV 'mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies' and ASV 'my desire' both add a word that is not there; Radak supplies 'what I desired'. The Hebrew can be heard as triumph, or as simple relief at being able to look them in the face. Malbim says that David did not need to fight them, since God rescued him without bloodshed, and Malbim ties it to the story in which a messenger tells Saul that the Philistines have invaded (1 Samuel 23:27). 'Trouble' is צָרָה, from the root for narrowness, a tight place, which pairs with the 'room' of salvation in verse 3. The picture to hold is a man who was hemmed in and now stands in the open and looks his enemies in the eye.

philological_notes.note: 'Trouble, distress', literally narrowness, being hemmed in; the opposite of the open space of rescue.
'My eye has looked'. No object is stated; Radak reads 'what I desired', Metzudat David 'what it wished to see in them'.
